event_hypothesis: The consul M. Aemilius, after subduing the Ligurians, built a road from Placentia to Ariminum and joined it to the Via Flaminia.

witnesses.quote_la: uiam Placentia usque Ariminum productam Flaminia iunxit

notes: Public-works event (road construction, the later Via Aemilia). Single witness, single Livian lineage. No corroboration in Florus, Eutropius, Orosius, or Obsequens.

event_hypothesis: Contemporaries dated the beginnings of luxury at Rome to the return of the army from Asia, which introduced it into the city.

witnesses.quote_la: Initia luxuriae in urbem introducta ab exercitu Asiatico referuntur

notes: Moralizing aition rather than a discrete event; 'referuntur' marks it as reported tradition even within the epitome. Likely tied to the triumph/return of Cn. Manlius Vulso's Asian army (187 BCE), but the Periocha names no commander.

event_hypothesis: The Bacchanalia, a nocturnal Greek rite, grew into a conspiracy of a huge multitude and was investigated and suppressed by the state with the punishment of many participants (186 BCE).

witnesses.quote_la: cum ad ingentis turbae coniurationem peruenisset, inuestigatum et multorum poena sublatum est

notes: Periocha also characterizes the cult: 'Bacchanalia, sacrum Graecum et nocturnum, omnium scelerum seminarium'. Striking silence elsewhere in this witness set: Obsequens' entry under the consuls of 186 (Sp. Postumius Albinus, Q. Marcius Philippus) records only prodigies and the ejection of Gauls, not the Bacchanalia; Florus, Eutropius, Orosius omit it entirely. No magistrates, quaestio, or senatus consultum are named by the epitome; scale ('ingentis turbae', 'multorum poena') and state investigation are the only recoverable details.

event_hypothesis: L. Valerius Flaccus and M. Porcius Cato (praised as supreme in the arts of war and peace) held the censorship together (184 BCE).

witnesses.quote_la: A censoribus L. Valerio Flacco et M. Porcio Catone, et belli et pacis artibus maximo

notes: Censorial college attested only as the agent of the Flamininus expulsion; the epitome preserves no other acts of this censorship (no lectio details, contracts, or taxes). The encomium 'et belli et pacis artibus maximo' applies to Cato.

event_hypothesis: The censors expelled L. Quinctius Flamininus, brother of Titus, from the senate for killing a man at a banquet in his consular province of Gaul to gratify a lover, and Cato delivered a speech against him.

witnesses.quote_la: motus est senatu L. Quintius Flamininus, T. frater

notes: Censorial expulsion (quasi prominent-trial by censorial nota, not a court verdict). The Periocha itself transmits a double tradition on the victim: either Flamininus killed a Gaul with his own hand at the request of the boy Philippus the Carthaginian ('scorto nobili, Gallum quemdam sua manu occiderat'), or, 'ut quidam tradiderunt', he beheaded a condemned man at the request of a Placentine courtesan ('unum ex damnatis securi percusserat rogatus a meretrice Placentina'). Documentary note: 'Extat oratio M. Catonis in eum'.

event_hypothesis: Scipio Africanus died away from Rome, estranged from the ungrateful city, at Liternum (so the Periocha; Orosius says after long exile at 'Amiternum', of illness, in 183 BCE).

witnesses.quote_la: Scipio Literni decessit et, tamquam iungente fortuna circa idem tempus duo funera maximorum uirorum
Scipio Africanus ab ingrata sibi urbe diu exulans apud Amiternum oppidum morbo periit

notes: Two witnesses but one Livian lineage, so no independence gained. Divergences: place of death Liternum (Periocha) vs Amiternum (Orosius, probably corruption or confusion); Orosius adds explicit exile and the city's ingratitude ('ab ingrata sibi urbe diu exulans') and death by illness, and dates it under the consuls M. Claudius Marcellus and Q. Fabius Labeo (183 BCE); the Periocha gives no date but synchronizes the deaths of Scipio, Hannibal, and Philopoemen ('duo funera maximorum uirorum' with Hannibal, Philopoemen added as 'quoque'). The political backstory (trials of the Scipios, withdrawal from Rome) is implied by Orosius' exile language but not narrated in this witness set.

event_hypothesis: Roman colonies were founded at Potentia, Pisaurum, Mutina, and Parma.

witnesses.quote_la: Coloniae Potentia et Pisaurum et Mutina et Parma deductae sunt

notes: Four deductions grouped in one notice (Potentia and Pisaurum 184 BCE, Mutina and Parma 183 BCE by standard chronology; the Periocha gives no dates, commissioners, or colonist numbers). No corroboration in the other witnesses.

event_hypothesis: M. Fulvius (Nobilior) celebrated a triumph at Rome over the Aetolians in the consulship of Sp. Postumius Albinus and Q. Marcius Philippus (186 BCE).

witnesses.quote_la: Sp. Postumio Albino Q. Marcio Philippo consulibus M. Fulvius de Aetolis triumphavit

notes: Only witness is Eutropius 4.5, which supplies the consular date. A triumph is a domestic ceremonial-political event; any senatorial dispute over its award (plausible given the delay after the Aetolian war ended in 189) is not attested in this witness set. Periocha 39 omits it.

event_hypothesis: Gauls who had crossed the Alps into Italy were expelled without a battle (under the consuls of 186 BCE).

witnesses.quote_la: Galli qui Alpes transierunt in Italiam sine proelio eiecti

notes: Obsequens, entry under Sp. Postumius Albinus and Q. Marcius Philippus (A.U.C. 568 / 186 BCE). Classified domestic-political with hesitation: 'sine proelio' implies a senatorial/diplomatic expulsion of transalpine settlers from Italian soil rather than a military campaign. No other witness mentions it.
